intro: Deal a topic, an audience, and a constraint. Speak for two minutes. Re-deal any card you can't use twice in a row.
topics: why mornings are better than evenings
the case for taking the stairs
what a city owes its pigeons
why every child should learn to cook one dish perfectly
the dignity of waiting in line
in defense of the voicemail
why maps are better than directions
the last bookstore in town
what handwriting reveals
the ethics of the snooze button
why rivers make better borders than walls
a eulogy for a household appliance
the case against motivational posters
what airports teach us about hope
why everyone should memorize one poem
the noble history of the pocket
in praise of doing things badly
what the moon is actually for
why weather small talk matters
the perfect sandwich, defended
what we lose when we lose winter
the case for mandatory naps
why museums should be louder
an argument for leaving the party early
what dogs know that we don't
the tyranny of the group photo
why the second draft is the real first draft
in defense of getting lost
what a handshake promises
why silence is a public good
the campaign speech of a benevolent tyrant
instructions for being a good neighbor
what the ocean thinks of us
why we should bring back the intermission
a toast at your rival's retirement
the case for one universal holiday
audiences: a stadium crowd in the rain
the town council of a village you've never visited
new employees on their first morning
a wedding reception, glass in hand
an audience that disagrees but is listening
constraints: Begin three successive sentences with the same phrase (anaphora).
End three successive sentences on the same word (epistrophe).
Open and close your speech on the same word (epanalepsis).
Let each sentence pick up the last word of the one before (anadiplosis).
Build one contrast per sentence: not this, but that (antithesis).
Say something, reverse its terms, and land on the reversal (antimetabole).
One metaphor only — but extend it the entire time.
No metaphors at all. Only literal statements.
Ask at least three questions you never answer (rhetorical question).
Address someone or something that cannot answer (apostrophe).
Understate everything; nothing is allowed to be amazing (litotes and meiosis).
Overstate everything; nothing is allowed to be ordinary (hyperbole).
Deny that you will mention the very things you mention (apophasis).
Drop every 'and' and 'but' — pile clauses bare (asyndeton).
Use 'and' relentlessly — chain everything (polysyndeton).
No sentence longer than eight words.
Every sentence longer than twenty words, and under control.
Alternate one long sentence with one of three words or fewer.
Save the main clause of your first sentence for its very end (periodic).
Start plain, then add detail after detail after the main clause (cumulative).
Interrupt yourself twice — and recover — mid-sentence (parenthesis).
Correct yourself out loud at least twice: say it, take it back, say it better (correctio).
Break off one sentence in the middle and leave it broken (aposiopesis).
Only words a ten-year-old knows.
Only Saxon words: short, blunt, physical. No Latinate polish.
Repeat one word three times in a row at your moment of peak feeling (epizeuxis).
Give everything you mention a fixed descriptive tag, Homer-style (epithet).
End on an aphorism you invent on the spot.
